Read the article

Words in bold are our key words.

Falling for Autumn

Ten small ways to fall in love with autumn

Summer has ended, the days have become shorter and the air has turned crisp. Many people feel a little sad when this happens. But autumn has its own kind of magic. To romanticise a season means to notice the small, beautiful moments and make ordinary days feel special. Here are ten ideas. How many have you already tried?

1. Build a pile of autumn books

Have you ever made a reading list just for autumn? Choose a few books you have wanted to read for a long time and stack them next to your bed. Mysteries and ghost stories feel just right when it gets dark at six o’clock.

2. Make a playlist for the season

Music changes with the seasons. Which songs remind you of autumn? Collect the slow, moody or slightly spooky ones, and the nostalgic songs you have loved for years. Play them on your walk to school or while you cook.

3. Fill your kitchen with cinnamon and apples

Few smells are as comforting as apples and cinnamon. If you have never made an apple crumble, now is the perfect time. Or just add a pinch of cinnamon to your porridge or hot chocolate.

4. Wrap up in a cosy jumper

Everyone loves a big, soft jumper in October. Have you found your favourite one yet? Wrap up in it, make a warm drink, and you are ready for any chilly evening.

5. Light up the dark evenings

The clocks go back at the end of October, so it gets dark very early. A candle or a string of fairy lights makes a room feel warm and calm instead of gloomy.

6. Go on a leaf walk

By now, many trees have turned gold, copper and deep red. Head to a park or a wood and kick through the crunchy leaves. Have you ever looked for shiny conkers under a horse chestnut tree? Children in Britain have played with them for generations.

7. Decorate your space

You don’t need to spend much money. A few pine cones, a small pumpkin on the windowsill or a jar of leaves you have collected can change the whole feel of a room.

8. Carve a pumpkin

Carving a pumpkin is messy, silly and great fun. Have you ever tried it? Many people throw the seeds away, but roasted with a little salt, they make a tasty snack.

9. Create an autumn bucket list

A bucket list is a list of things you want to do before a certain time. What haven’t you done yet this year? Write down everything you want to enjoy before winter arrives, like fireworks on Bonfire Night, a new soup recipe or a trip to a pumpkin patch.

10. Bake cinnamon buns or pumpkin pie

Nothing makes a home feel cosier than the smell of baking. Cinnamon buns are soft, sweet and sticky, and pumpkin pie is a favourite in America at Thanksgiving. Have you ever baked either of them? If you haven’t, start with a simple recipe. Then invite a friend round, share what you have made, and enjoy it with a cup of tea.

Present perfect in the text

Why does the writer use the present perfect here? Is the time finished? Do we know exactly when? Sort the sentences into groups.

Have you found your favourite one yet?
Have you ever made a reading list just for autumn?
By now, many trees have turned gold, copper and deep red.
Children in Britain have played with them for generations.
…books you have wanted to read for a long time.
…a jar of leaves you have collected.
How many have you already tried?
Carving a pumpkin is great fun. Have you ever tried it?
If you have never made an apple crumble, now is the perfect time.
What haven’t you done yet this year?
Summer has ended, and the air has turned crisp.
…the nostalgic songs you have loved for years.
A. Life experienceever, never · we don’t say when it happened
B. Unfinished timefor, since · it started in the past and continues now
C. Up to nowalready, yet · has it happened before now?
D. Change or result nowsomething happened, and we see the result now
Grammar: answersSkudra Academy

Present perfect: answers

Each sentence in its group, plus the rule.

Formhave / has + past participle
I’ve (I have) tried · she’s (she has) made
I haven’t done it yet. · Have you ever…?
Present simple or present perfect?Present simple: habits and facts. Music changes with the seasons. It gets dark very early.
Present perfect: links the past to now. Summer has ended. Have you ever carved a pumpkin?
Have you ever made a reading list just for autumn?
If you have never made an apple crumble, now is the perfect time.
Carving a pumpkin is great fun. Have you ever tried it?
…books you have wanted to read for a long time.
…the nostalgic songs you have loved for years.
Children in Britain have played with them for generations.
How many have you already tried?
Have you found your favourite one yet?
What haven’t you done yet this year?
Summer has ended, and the air has turned crisp.
By now, many trees have turned gold, copper and deep red.
…a jar of leaves you have collected.
A. Life experienceever, never · we don’t say when it happened
B. Unfinished timefor, since · it started in the past and continues now
C. Up to nowalready, yet · has it happened before now?
D. Change or result nowsomething happened, and we see the result now

SpeakSkudra Academy

Let’s talk!

Answer, then add one more detail.

Present simple

1What do you usually do on a cold autumn evening?
2Which season do you like best, and why?
3What food or drink reminds you of autumn?
4How does the weather change in autumn where you come from?
5Do you prefer a cosy night in or a walk outside? Why?
6What does autumn smell, sound and look like to you?

Present perfect

1Have you ever carved a pumpkin? How did it go?
2Have you ever been to a Bonfire Night fireworks display?
3What is the best book you have read this year?
4Which ideas from the article have you already tried?
5How has autumn in the UK been different from autumn in your home country?
6What haven’t you done yet this year that you really want to do?

Mixed

1Have you made an autumn bucket list? What is on it?
2Which song have you listened to most this month, and why do you like it?
3What is one thing you have never done in autumn but want to try?
TipHave you ever…? → Yes, I have! I went last year. It was amazing.
